catalog_citation: Blust, Robert. 2003. A short morphology, phonology and vocabulary of Kiput, Sarawak. Pacific Linguistics 546. Canberra: Pacific Linguistics, RSPAS, Australian National University. viii+102 pp. DOI 10.15144/PL-546 (open CC BY-SA online edition).
catalog_locator: Chapter 1 'Discussion', section 4 'Phonology', 4.3.2 'Stress', pp. 26-27; supporting 4.3.3 p. 27 and 4.4.4 p. 37.
catalog_quote: 4.3.2 Stress. As in many other languages in the coastal and lowland areas of central and northern Sarawak, stress is final in citation forms. However, unlike some languages of the region in which the final stress of citation forms varies with penultimate stress in phrasal forms, word-stress in Kiput appears to remain final throughout. Some Kiput forms appear to show stress contrasts, but both synchronic and historical information show that these are better analyzed as contrasts of tautosyllabic vs. heterosyllabic sequences of similar vocoids. The former sequences constitute diphthongs, as noted above, and in these stress falls on the vowel preceding the non-syllabic schwa, as in lufiep 'tide', pafiet 'kind of bat', bawieng 'onion', mabue' 'drunk', soe 'rice mortar', or manoe' 'bird'. The latter sequences, by contrast, constitute two separate vowels, as in buen 'bottom', muek 'enter', puet 'navel', meliem 'dark', meriem 'cannon', tekien 'thread' or tuew 'right side', or lipeh tuew 'python', all of which are stressed on the schwa preceding the final consonant. [4.3.3, p. 27] The vowels I, U and e (schwa) are invariably short, as are all vowels in unstressed (non-final) syllables and all vowels preceding word-final h. [4.4.4, p. 37] Historically the inherited vowels *i, *u and *a were lengthened in stressed (hence final) syllables.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls on the final syllable, both in citation forms and in phrasal context (no penultimate shift in connected speech, unlike some neighbouring Sarawak languages). Where a word ends in a falling diphthong with a non-syllabic schwa offglide (lufiep, manoe'), stress is on the vowel before the offglide, i.e. still the final syllable nucleus; where the vowel + schwa sequence is heterosyllabic (buen, meliem), stress is on the schwa of the final syllable.
new_statements.exceptions: Apparent stress contrasts (e.g. meliem 'dark' with stress on final schwa vs. miciem 'to borrow' with stress on the high front vowel) are reanalysed as diphthong vs. two-vowel sequences rather than lexical stress; author hedges with 'appears to remain final throughout'. Vowels in unstressed (non-final) syllables are always short (section 4.3.3, p. 27).
new_statements.domain_note: Explicitly addresses both citation forms and phrasal forms: final in citation forms and 'appears to remain final throughout' (i.e. also phrase-medially). Data from one principal speaker (John Malang), Kiput of the lower Baram, northern Sarawak.
new_statements.identity_note: Source describes Kiput (ISO kyi, kipu1237) as spoken at the mouth of the Baram River, northern Sarawak, from fieldwork principally with one speaker (John Malang); no dialect subdivision named. Matches the target languoid directly.
